Terrified
ter'ri-fide
v. (struck with terror; forbidden to soldiers before battle, to the church before its adversaries, and felt by the disciples in the presence of the risen Christ)
From Latin terrere, to frighten, through terrificare, to make afraid. The Hebrew at Deuteronomy 20:3 is arats, to tremble or be terrified; the Greek at Philippians 1:28 is pturo, to be startled — a word used of horses shying.

Biblical Definition

Twice the word appears in a prohibition, which is worth pausing over: God commands men not to be terrified. In the priest's address before battle: “Hear, O Israel, ye approach this day unto battle against your enemies: let not your hearts faint, fear not, and do not tremble, neither be ye terrified because of them” (Deuteronomy 20:3) — and the reason follows, that the LORD goeth with them to fight for them. Our Lord gives the same command about the end: “when ye shall hear of wars and commotions, be not terrified: for these things must first come to pass; but the end is not by and by” (Luke 21:9). Paul makes composure under opposition itself a sign: “And in nothing terrified by your adversaries: which is to them an evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation, and that of God” (Philippians 1:28). The Greek pturo is the word for a horse shying at a shadow, and Paul says the church's failure to shy is legible to its enemies. The fourth occurrence is honest about how hard the command is: when the risen Christ stood among them, “they were terrified and affrighted, and supposed that they had seen a spirit” (Luke 24:37).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines terrify as to frighten, to alarm or shock with fear — and notes it is a stronger word than merely to fear.

TERRIFIED, pp. Frightened; affrighted.

TERRIFY, v.t. To frighten; to alarm or shock with fear.

When ye shall hear of wars, be not terrified. Luke 21.

TERRIBLE, a. Frightful; adapted to excite terror; dreadful; formidable.

TERROR, n. Extreme fear; violent dread; fright; fear that agitates the body and mind.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 20:3 — "And shall say unto them, Hear, O Israel, ye approach this day unto battle against your enemies: let not your hearts faint, fear not, and do not tremble, neither be ye terrified because of them;"

Luke 21:9 — "But when ye shall hear of wars and commotions, be not terrified: for these things must first come to pass; but the end is not by and by."

Philippians 1:28 — "And in nothing terrified by your adversaries: which is to them an evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation, and that of God."

Luke 24:37 — "But they were terrified and affrighted, and supposed that they had seen a spirit."

Modern Corruption

Fear is treated as involuntary and therefore beyond command, which makes the many biblical prohibitions of it unintelligible.

expand to see more

If fear is purely a physiological reflex, then be not terrified is as sensible as commanding a man not to sneeze, and the hundred-odd fear not sayings of Scripture become well-meant encouragement rather than commands. The Bible treats fear as genuinely commandable, and it does so by always attaching a ground. Deuteronomy 20 does not say be brave; it says the LORD your God goeth with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you. Luke 21 does not say the wars are trivial; it says these things must first come to pass — they are inside a plan. Fear is addressed at the level of what a man believes to be true, which is why the remedy is always a fact and never a technique.

Luke 24:37 keeps the doctrine honest. The eleven, hearing the very reports they had hoped for, saw Christ and were terrified — and He did not rebuke them for it as though terror were sin. He showed them His hands and His feet, invited them to handle Him, ate a piece of broiled fish before them, and opened their understanding that they might understand the scriptures. That is the pastoral pattern: the answer to fear is evidence and Scripture, patiently given. Philippians 1:28 states what such settled fearlessness eventually becomes — a token, legible to adversaries, that this salvation is of God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew arats, to tremble, be terrified — Deuteronomy 20:3; Greek ptoeo, to be startled — Luke 21:9, 24:37; pturo, to shy as a frightened horse — Philippians 1:28.

expand to see more

Hebrew arats — to tremble, dread, be terrified; Deuteronomy 20:3 and Joshua 1:9.

Greek ptoeo — to be startled or terrified; Luke 21:9 and Luke 24:37.

Greek pturo — to be frightened as a horse shying; Philippians 1:28, its only New Testament occurrence.

Greek endeixis — an evident token or proof; what the church's composure becomes.

Latin terrere, to frighten — the source of the English word.

Usage

"“Neither be ye terrified because of them” — a command, with a reason attached."

"“In nothing terrified by your adversaries” — composure legible as a token."

"“They were terrified and affrighted” — and He showed them His hands and His feet."
